fp1_vectors_products.description: Find a vector product, check its orientation and use it to calculate area, height, volume or coplanarity in three dimensions.

sections.title: How do I find a vector perpendicular to two directions?
sections.label: Use the vector product
sections.intro: The vector product takes two directions in three dimensions and gives a signed normal.

blocks.html: Form the component differences in cyclic order. Check zero scalar products with both original vectors.

blocks.title: Compute the right-handed vector product
blocks.prompt: Find \(\mathbf u\times\mathbf v\) for \(\mathbf u=\left[\begin{matrix}3\\1\\-1\end{matrix}\right]\) and \(\mathbf v=\left[\begin{matrix}1\\-2\\3\end{matrix}\right]\).
blocks.hint: Organise the three component differences in cyclic order.
blocks.solution:
Use the component differences from the two rows. The first is \(3\) minus \(2\).

The full vector product is \(\left[\begin{matrix}1\\-10\\-7\end{matrix}\right]\).

Its dot products with both original vectors are zero. Its direction also depends on the order.

blocks.html: A scalar product returns a number. A vector product returns a three-component direction.

sections.title: What changes if I reverse the order?
sections.label: Check orientation separately
sections.intro: Orientation follows the right-hand rule from the first direction to the second.

blocks.html: \(\mathbf v\times\mathbf u=-(\mathbf u\times\mathbf v)\). The magnitudes agree.

blocks.title: Reverse the normal when the order of vectors changes
blocks.prompt: The vector \(\mathbf u\times\mathbf v\) is \(\left[\begin{matrix}1\\-10\\-7\end{matrix}\right]\). Find the x- and z-components of \(\mathbf v\times\mathbf u\).
blocks.hint: Negate every component, without reversing the order of the components.
blocks.solution:
Reversing the factor order reverses the right-handed direction.

The new vector is \(\left[\begin{matrix}-1\\10\\7\end{matrix}\right]\). Its magnitude is unchanged.

The requested x- and z-components are \(-1\) and \(7\).

blocks.html: Negate all three components without changing their positions.

sections.title: How does the vector product give a triangle area?
sections.label: Take half the magnitude
sections.intro: Two side displacements from one vertex make a parallelogram. The triangle covers half of it.

blocks.html: Use half the magnitude of the vector product. Use displacements having the same starting vertex.

blocks.title: Use half the parallelogram area for a triangle
blocks.prompt: Find the area of triangle ABC with \(A=\)\(\left(2,2,0\right)\), \(B=\)\(\left(5,2,0\right)\) and \(C=\)\(\left(3,6,0\right)\).
blocks.hint: Use vectors sharing the same starting vertex.
blocks.solution:
Use the two vectors measured from A: \(\left[\begin{matrix}3\\0\\0\end{matrix}\right]\) and \(\left[\begin{matrix}1\\4\\0\end{matrix}\right]\).

Their cross product is \(\left[\begin{matrix}0\\0\\12\end{matrix}\right]\). Its magnitude is the parallelogram area.

The triangle occupies half that area, giving \(6\).

blocks.html: Vector components can be signed. Area is non-negative.

blocks.title: Use half the parallelogram area for a triangle
blocks.prompt: Find the area of triangle ABC with \(A=\)\(\left(4,2,0\right)\), \(B=\)\(\left(9,2,0\right)\) and \(C=\)\(\left(5,8,0\right)\).
blocks.hint: Use vectors sharing the same starting vertex.
blocks.solution:
Use the two vectors measured from A: \(\left[\begin{matrix}5\\0\\0\end{matrix}\right]\) and \(\left[\begin{matrix}1\\6\\0\end{matrix}\right]\).

Their cross product is \(\left[\begin{matrix}0\\0\\30\end{matrix}\right]\). Its magnitude is the parallelogram area.

The triangle occupies half that area, giving \(15\).

sections.title: How can I test a fourth point for coplanarity?
sections.label: Test its displacement against a normal
sections.intro: Three non-collinear points determine a plane. Find its non-zero normal from two displacements.

blocks.html: The fourth point is coplanar if its displacement from the same reference point has zero dot product with the normal.

blocks.title: Use a scalar product with a cross-product normal
blocks.prompt: The points \(A=\)\(\left(2,0,0\right)\), \(B=\)\(\left(3,0,1\right)\), \(C=\)\(\left(2,2,1\right)\) and \(D=\)\(\left(k,3,4\right)\) are coplanar. Find \(k\).
blocks.hint: Use displacements from the same reference point.
blocks.solution:
The first three points are not collinear because the cross product of their two direction vectors is \(\left[\begin{matrix}-2\\-1\\2\end{matrix}\right]\).

The displacement from A to D lies in their plane if its dot product with this normal is zero.

Solve \(9 - 2 k=0\) to obtain \(k=\frac{9}{2}\).

blocks.html: If the original directions are parallel, their zero vector product cannot define a plane.

sections.title: How can a vector product help find a tetrahedron volume?
sections.label: Use base area and normal height
sections.intro: The base triangle has half the cross-product magnitude as its area. Project the fourth point onto the same normal to find the height.

blocks.html: The volume is one sixth of the absolute scalar triple product. The factor combines triangle and pyramid factors.

blocks.title: Find tetrahedron volume from a projected height
blocks.prompt: Find the volume of the tetrahedron with vertices at the origin, \(\left(3,0,0\right)\), \(\left(0,4,0\right)\) and \(\left(1,2,2\right)\).
blocks.hint: Use the absolute volume, then account for both the triangular base and pyramid factor.
blocks.solution:
Use the first two displacements for the base triangle. The cross-product magnitude gives twice its area.

The height of the last point above the base plane is the magnitude of its normal projection.

One third of base area times height gives \(4\). Equivalently take one sixth of the absolute scalar triple product.

blocks.html: The signed triple product may be negative. The volume cannot be.

blocks.title: Find tetrahedron volume from a projected height
blocks.prompt: Find the volume of the tetrahedron with vertices at the origin, \(\left(5,0,0\right)\), \(\left(0,6,0\right)\) and \(\left(1,2,4\right)\).
blocks.hint: Use the absolute volume, then account for both the triangular base and pyramid factor.
blocks.solution:

The height of the last point above the base plane is the magnitude of its normal projection.

One third of base area times height gives \(20\). Equivalently take one sixth of the absolute scalar triple product.

examples.title: Reverse the normal when the order of vectors changes

The new vector is \(\left[\begin{matrix}0\\5\\5\end{matrix}\right]\). Its magnitude is unchanged.
The requested x- and z-components are \(0\) and \(5\).

examples.title: Use half the parallelogram area for a triangle
examples.question: Find the area of triangle ABC with \(A=\)\(\left(1,2,0\right)\), \(B=\)\(\left(3,2,0\right)\) and \(C=\)\(\left(2,5,0\right)\).
solution: Use the two vectors measured from A: \(\left[\begin{matrix}2\\0\\0\end{matrix}\right]\) and \(\left[\begin{matrix}1\\3\\0\end{matrix}\right]\).
Their cross product is \(\left[\begin{matrix}0\\0\\6\end{matrix}\right]\). Its magnitude is the parallelogram area.
The triangle occupies half that area, giving \(3\).

examples.question: The points \(A=\)\(\left(1,0,0\right)\), \(B=\)\(\left(2,0,1\right)\), \(C=\)\(\left(1,2,1\right)\) and \(D=\)\(\left(k,2,3\right)\) are coplanar. Find \(k\).

fp1_vectors_lines.description: Check line membership and intersections using independent parameters. Locate feet and common perpendiculars by scalar products.

sections.title: How can I tell whether a point is on a line?
sections.label: Use one parameter for all coordinates
sections.intro: A known point and one non-zero direction specify the line. The parameter selects the position.

blocks.html: Solve a coordinate with non-zero direction component and then check the others at that same parameter.

blocks.title: Use one line parameter in all three coordinates
blocks.prompt: Does \(\left(3,1,5\right)\) lie on \(\mathbf r=\left[\begin{matrix}2\\-1\\2\end{matrix}\right]+t\left[\begin{matrix}1\\2\\2\end{matrix}\right]\)? Give the parameter obtained from the x-coordinate and decide.

fields.label: Does the point lie on the line?

blocks.hint: Check the same value in every coordinate, including any constant coordinate.
blocks.solution:
The first coordinate fixes the candidate parameter at \(1\).

The same parameter must also produce the y- and z-coordinates.

Substitution into the whole vector equation gives \(\left(3,1,4\right)\). The third coordinate differs from the given point, so it is not on the line.

blocks.html: Even a constant coordinate must be checked for membership.

sections.title: What determines a common point of two lines?
sections.label: Use a separate parameter on each line
sections.intro: A common point need not occur at the same value of both parameters.

blocks.html: Solve two coordinate equalities, check the third and give the point.

blocks.title: Solve for separate parameters at a common point
blocks.prompt: Find both parameters and the x-coordinate where \(\mathbf r=\left[\begin{matrix}2\\-1\\2\end{matrix}\right]+s\left[\begin{matrix}1\\2\\2\end{matrix}\right]\) and \(\mathbf r=\left[\begin{matrix}1\\7\\6\end{matrix}\right]+t\left[\begin{matrix}2\\-1\\1\end{matrix}\right]\) intersect.
blocks.hint: Solve two equations, then use the third as an independent check.
blocks.solution:
Set the three coordinate equations equal. The two parameters refer to different lines.

Solving the first two equations gives \(s=3\) and \(t=2\). The third equation agrees.

Substitution gives the common point \(\left(5,5,8\right)\).

blocks.html: Solving just two equations might leave the third unsatisfied.

sections.title: What makes two non-parallel lines skew?
sections.label: Check the whole position
sections.intro: Two non-parallel lines have at most one common point. If its third coordinate fails, the lines are skew.

blocks.html: A non-zero scalar triple product of both directions with a displacement between the lines also proves they are skew.

blocks.title: Decide when non-parallel lines are skew
blocks.prompt: For lines \(\mathbf r=\left[\begin{matrix}2\\-1\\2\end{matrix}\right]+s\left[\begin{matrix}1\\2\\2\end{matrix}\right]\) and \(\mathbf r=\left[\begin{matrix}3\\6\\10\end{matrix}\right]+t\left[\begin{matrix}2\\-1\\1\end{matrix}\right]\), solve equality of x- and y-coordinates. Do the lines intersect?

fields.label: Value of s from x and y
Value of t from x and y

blocks.hint: A solution to two coordinate equations need not satisfy the third.
blocks.solution:
The directional vectors are not parallel. Solve the x and y equations to get \(s=3\) and \(t=1\).

At these values the z-coordinates differ by \(3\).

There is no common point, so these non-parallel lines are skew.

blocks.html: Non-parallel lines in space need not cross.

blocks.title: Decide when non-parallel lines are skew
blocks.prompt: For lines \(\mathbf r=\left[\begin{matrix}4\\-1\\2\end{matrix}\right]+s\left[\begin{matrix}1\\2\\4\end{matrix}\right]\) and \(\mathbf r=\left[\begin{matrix}7\\10\\26\end{matrix}\right]+t\left[\begin{matrix}2\\-1\\1\end{matrix}\right]\), solve equality of x- and y-coordinates. Do the lines intersect?

fields.label: Value of s from x and y
Value of t from x and y

blocks.hint: A solution to two coordinate equations need not satisfy the third.
blocks.solution:
The directional vectors are not parallel. Solve the x and y equations to get \(s=5\) and \(t=1\).

At these values the z-coordinates differ by \(5\).

There is no common point, so these non-parallel lines are skew.

sections.title: How do I find the nearest point on a line?
sections.label: Impose perpendicularity
sections.intro: Take a variable point on the line. The shortest segment to the external point is perpendicular to its direction.

blocks.html: Solve the zero scalar-product equation to find the foot parameter and calculate the joining vector length.

blocks.title: Find a foot by imposing perpendicularity
blocks.prompt: From point \(\left(6,-3,2\right)\), find the foot on \(\mathbf r=\left[\begin{matrix}2\\-1\\2\end{matrix}\right]+t\left[\begin{matrix}1\\2\\2\end{matrix}\right]\) and the shortest distance. Give the foot parameter and exact distance.

fields.label: Value of t at the foot

blocks.hint: Use a scalar product to find the parameter, then measure the length of the perpendicular segment.
blocks.solution:
Let the foot be on the line with parameter t. Its vector to the given point must be perpendicular to the line’s direction.

Set the scalar product to zero and solve, giving \(t=0\). The foot is \(\left(2,-1,2\right)\).

The joining vector is \(\left[\begin{matrix}4\\-2\\0\end{matrix}\right]\), whose magnitude is \(2 \sqrt{5}\).

blocks.html: Matching just one coordinate does not normally give the perpendicular foot.

sections.title: How do I find the shortest join between skew lines?
sections.label: Use both perpendicular equations
sections.intro: Take a variable point on each line. The shortest joining vector is perpendicular to both line directions.

blocks.html: Use two zero scalar products to find the endpoint parameters. If the directions are parallel instead, project a displacement perpendicular to one of them.

figure.caption: The shortest joining segment is perpendicular to both spatial directions.
figure.alt: Two skew lines with a dashed shortest segment joining one point on each line, drawn schematically.

blocks.title: Find both ends of a common perpendicular
blocks.prompt: Find the parameters of the endpoints of the common perpendicular between \(\mathbf r=\left[\begin{matrix}0\\0\\0\end{matrix}\right]+s\left[\begin{matrix}1\\0\\0\end{matrix}\right]\) and \(\mathbf r=\left[\begin{matrix}0\\2\\3\end{matrix}\right]+t\left[\begin{matrix}0\\1\\0\end{matrix}\right]\). Give its length.
blocks.hint: Write the vector joining arbitrary points, then impose both perpendicular conditions.
blocks.solution:
If the joining vector is perpendicular to both directions, it has zero x- and y-components here.

The x-coordinate condition gives \(s=0\) and the y-coordinate condition gives \(t=-2\).

The endpoints then differ only in z, with length \(3\).

blocks.html: A zero vector product cannot define a skew-line normal. Classify the lines before normalising.

blocks.title: Find both ends of a common perpendicular
blocks.prompt: Find the parameters of the endpoints of the common perpendicular between \(\mathbf r=\left[\begin{matrix}0\\0\\0\end{matrix}\right]+s\left[\begin{matrix}1\\0\\0\end{matrix}\right]\) and \(\mathbf r=\left[\begin{matrix}0\\4\\5\end{matrix}\right]+t\left[\begin{matrix}0\\1\\0\end{matrix}\right]\). Give its length.
blocks.hint: Write the vector joining arbitrary points, then impose both perpendicular conditions.
blocks.solution:
If the joining vector is perpendicular to both directions, it has zero x- and y-components here.

The x-coordinate condition gives \(s=0\) and the y-coordinate condition gives \(t=-4\).

The endpoints then differ only in z, with length \(5\).

examples.title: Use one line parameter in all three coordinates
examples.question: Does \(\left(3,3,4\right)\) lie on \(\mathbf r=\left[\begin{matrix}1\\-1\\2\end{matrix}\right]+t\left[\begin{matrix}1\\2\\1\end{matrix}\right]\)? Give the parameter obtained from the x-coordinate and decide.
solution: The first coordinate fixes the candidate parameter at \(2\).
The same parameter must also produce the y- and z-coordinates.
Substitution into the whole vector equation gives \(\left(3,3,4\right)\). This is the given point.

examples.question: Find both parameters and the x-coordinate where \(\mathbf r=\left[\begin{matrix}1\\-1\\2\end{matrix}\right]+s\left[\begin{matrix}1\\2\\1\end{matrix}\right]\) and \(\mathbf r=\left[\begin{matrix}1\\4\\3\end{matrix}\right]+t\left[\begin{matrix}2\\-1\\1\end{matrix}\right]\) intersect.
solution: Set the three coordinate equations equal. The two parameters refer to different lines.
Solving the first two equations gives \(s=2\) and \(t=1\). The third equation agrees.
Substitution gives the common point \(\left(3,3,4\right)\).

examples.title: Decide when non-parallel lines are skew
examples.question: For lines \(\mathbf r=\left[\begin{matrix}1\\-1\\2\end{matrix}\right]+s\left[\begin{matrix}1\\2\\1\end{matrix}\right]\) and \(\mathbf r=\left[\begin{matrix}1\\4\\5\end{matrix}\right]+t\left[\begin{matrix}2\\-1\\1\end{matrix}\right]\), solve equality of x- and y-coordinates. Do the lines intersect?
solution: The directional vectors are not parallel. Solve the x and y equations to get \(s=2\) and \(t=1\).
At these values the z-coordinates differ by \(2\).
There is no common point, so these non-parallel lines are skew.

examples.title: Decide when non-parallel lines are skew
examples.question: For lines \(\mathbf r=\left[\begin{matrix}3\\-1\\2\end{matrix}\right]+s\left[\begin{matrix}1\\2\\3\end{matrix}\right]\) and \(\mathbf r=\left[\begin{matrix}5\\8\\17\end{matrix}\right]+t\left[\begin{matrix}2\\-1\\1\end{matrix}\right]\), solve equality of x- and y-coordinates. solution: The directional vectors are not parallel. Solve the x and y equations to get \(s=4\) and \(t=1\).
At these values the z-coordinates differ by \(4\).
There is no common point, so these non-parallel lines are skew.

examples.title: Find a foot by imposing perpendicularity
examples.question: From point \(\left(2,-4,1\right)\), find the foot on \(\mathbf r=\left[\begin{matrix}1\\-1\\2\end{matrix}\right]+t\left[\begin{matrix}1\\2\\1\end{matrix}\right]\) and the shortest distance. Give the foot parameter and exact distance.
solution: Let the foot be on the line with parameter t. Its vector to the given point must be perpendicular to the line’s direction.
Set the scalar product to zero and solve, giving \(t=-1\). The foot is \(\left(0,-3,1\right)\).
The joining vector is \(\left[\begin{matrix}2\\-1\\0\end{matrix}\right]\), whose magnitude is \(\sqrt{5}\).

examples.title: Find both ends of a common perpendicular
examples.question: Find the parameters of the endpoints of the common perpendicular between \(\mathbf r=\left[\begin{matrix}0\\0\\0\end{matrix}\right]+s\left[\begin{matrix}1\\0\\0\end{matrix}\right]\) and \(\mathbf r=\left[\begin{matrix}0\\1\\2\end{matrix}\right]+t\left[\begin{matrix}0\\1\\0\end{matrix}\right]\). Give its length.
solution: If the joining vector is perpendicular to both directions, it has zero x- and y-components here.
The x-coordinate condition gives \(s=0\) and the y-coordinate condition gives \(t=-1\).
The endpoints then differ only in z, with length \(2\).

examples.title: Find both ends of a common perpendicular
examples.question: Find the parameters of the endpoints of the common perpendicular between \(\mathbf r=\left[\begin{matrix}0\\0\\0\end{matrix}\right]+s\left[\begin{matrix}1\\0\\0\end{matrix}\right]\) and \(\mathbf r=\left[\begin{matrix}0\\3\\4\end{matrix}\right]+t\left[\begin{matrix}0\\1\\0\end{matrix}\right]\). Give its length.
solution: If the joining vector is perpendicular to both directions, it has zero x- and y-components here.
The x-coordinate condition gives \(s=0\) and the y-coordinate condition gives \(t=-3\).
The endpoints then differ only in z, with length \(4\).

fp1_vectors_planes.description: Convert between plane forms, find intersections with lines or planes and identify parallel and coincident cases.

sections.title: What determines a plane from three points?
sections.label: Find two independent displacements
sections.intro: Use displacements from the same reference point. Their vector product is a normal unless the three points are collinear.

blocks.html: Dot the normal with a known point to find the constant of the Cartesian equation.

blocks.title: Build a normal from two in-plane directions
blocks.prompt: The plane contains \(\left(2,2,-1\right)\), \(\left(3,3,-1\right)\) and \(\left(2,3,1\right)\). Use \(\overrightarrow{AB}\times\overrightarrow{AC}\) as the normal. Give its components and the right-hand constant in the Cartesian equation.
blocks.hint: Use point differences before computing the cross product.
blocks.solution:
Form two displacements from the first point. They are \(\left[\begin{matrix}1\\1\\0\end{matrix}\right]\) and \(\left[\begin{matrix}0\\1\\2\end{matrix}\right]\).

Their cross product is \(\left[\begin{matrix}2\\-2\\1\end{matrix}\right]\), which is non-zero and perpendicular to the plane.

Take its dot product with a known point to find the constant \(-1\). The equation is \(2 x - 2 y + z=-1\).

blocks.html: A normal determines orientation, while the plane position also requires an offset.

sections.title: How do the parametric and scalar-product forms agree?
sections.label: Remove both direction terms
sections.intro: Two independent directions span the plane through a known point. Its normal is perpendicular to both.

blocks.html: Dot the entire vector equation with the normal. The parameter terms vanish and the fixed offset remains.

blocks.title: Convert a parametric plane to a scalar-product equation
blocks.prompt: The plane is \(\mathbf r=\left[\begin{matrix}2\\2\\-1\end{matrix}\right]+s\left[\begin{matrix}1\\1\\0\end{matrix}\right]+t\left[\begin{matrix}0\\1\\2\end{matrix}\right]\). Find the constant and the z coefficient in its Cartesian equation, using the normal \(\left[\begin{matrix}2\\-2\\1\end{matrix}\right]\).
blocks.hint: Dot the entire vector equation with the normal, including its offset.
blocks.solution:
The offset point is \(\left(2,2,-1\right)\). The supplied normal is perpendicular to the two direction vectors.

Taking the dot product with the normal sends both direction terms to zero.

The remaining constant is \(-1\). The equivalent Cartesian equation is \(2 x - 2 y + z=-1\).

blocks.html: Two parallel directions do not span a plane.

sections.title: Why do non-parallel planes meet in a line?
sections.label: Use both equations at once
sections.intro: Independent planes give two simultaneous conditions in three coordinates.

blocks.html: Eliminate one coordinate to obtain an anchor and direction. The line direction is perpendicular to both normals.

blocks.title: Subtract two plane equations to expose a line
blocks.prompt: Find the fixed y-coordinate and the z-coordinate when \(x=0\) on the intersection of \(x + y + z=5\) and \(x - y + z=1\).
blocks.hint: Eliminate a coordinate and keep one free parameter for the intersection line.
blocks.solution:
Subtract the equations. This gives \(2y=4\), hence \(y=2\).

Substitute back to get \(x+z=3\). The intersection is the line satisfying both equations.

At \(x=0\) its z-coordinate is \(3\).

blocks.html: The direction alone does not specify where the line lies.

blocks.title: Subtract two plane equations to expose a line
blocks.prompt: Find the fixed y-coordinate and the z-coordinate when \(x=0\) on the intersection of \(x + y + z=9\) and \(x - y + z=1\).
blocks.hint: Eliminate a coordinate and keep one free parameter for the intersection line.
blocks.solution:
Subtract the equations. This gives \(2y=8\), hence \(y=4\).

Substitute back to get \(x+z=5\). The intersection is the line satisfying both equations.

At \(x=0\) its z-coordinate is \(5\).

sections.title: When does a line meet a plane once?
sections.label: Solve for its line parameter
sections.intro: A line substituted into the plane gives one equation in its parameter.

blocks.html: A non-zero coefficient gives a unique crossing. If the coefficient is zero, compare the constants to distinguish contained and parallel cases.

blocks.title: Substitute a line into a plane equation
blocks.prompt: Find the line parameter and the z-coordinate at the intersection of \(\mathbf r=\left[\begin{matrix}2\\2\\-1\end{matrix}\right]+t\left[\begin{matrix}1\\2\\-1\end{matrix}\right]\) and \(2 x - 2 y + z=-10\).
blocks.hint: Insert the complete line coordinates into the plane instead of comparing direction vectors alone.
blocks.solution:
Substituting the line into the plane equation gives one linear equation in the parameter.

The coefficient of the parameter is \(-3\), non-zero, so the solution is unique.

Solving gives \(t=3\). The intersection is \(\left(5,8,-4\right)\).

blocks.html: Checking the direction alone cannot tell whether a parallel line lies in the plane.

sections.title: How can parallel equations name the same plane?
sections.label: Scale all coefficients consistently
sections.intro: Parallel normals give a shared orientation. Plane locations may still differ.

blocks.html: To test coincidence, multiply the entire equation by the same non-zero factor, including its right-hand constant.

blocks.title: Distinguish different parallel planes from one plane twice
blocks.prompt: Are \(x + 2 y - z=3\) and \(3 x + 6 y - 3 z=10\) the same plane? Give the multiplier relating the second normal to the first.
blocks.hint: Scale the entire equation, including its right-hand constant, before comparing.
blocks.solution:
The normal of the second plane is \(3\) times the normal of the first. The planes are parallel or coincident.

Apply the same multiplier to the right-hand constant. It gives \(9\).

This differs from the second constant, so the planes are distinct and parallel.

fp1_vectors_distances.description: Choose a perpendicular component for a distance, find a reflection, and compare line and plane angles.

sections.title: How do I convert a plane equation into a distance?
sections.label: Project along a normal
sections.intro: Subtract the plane’s constant from the scalar product at the given point. The result is the signed excess along a non-unit normal.

blocks.html: Divide its magnitude by the length of the normal. Find the foot by moving along the normal line to the plane.

figure.caption: Move along the normal to reach the closest point on the plane.
figure.alt: Point P is above a plane. A dashed normal segment ends at the foot on the plane.

blocks.title: Project a point onto the normal of the plane
blocks.prompt: Find the shortest distance from \(\left(5,8,9\right)\) to \(x + 2 y + 2 z=12\) and the x-coordinate of its foot.
blocks.hint: The normal is not necessarily a unit vector. Divide by its magnitude for a distance.
blocks.solution:
The signed normal excess is \(\mathbf n\cdot\mathbf p-d=27\).

Divide by the magnitude of the normal to find distance \(9\).

Move along the negative normal to the plane. The foot is \(\left(2,2,3\right)\).

blocks.html: Using the normal excess itself as a distance misses its scale unless the normal is a unit vector.

sections.title: How does a perpendicular foot give a reflection?
sections.label: Continue beyond the foot by the same displacement
sections.intro: The line between a point and its reflection is perpendicular to the plane. Its midpoint lies on the plane.

blocks.html: The reflection’s vector is twice the foot vector minus the original point vector.

blocks.title: Use the foot as the midpoint of a reflection
blocks.prompt: Reflect \(\left(4,6,7\right)\) across \(x + 2 y + 2 z=12\). Give the resulting Cartesian coordinates.
blocks.hint: After finding the foot, continue the same displacement once more.
blocks.solution:
A perpendicular through the point meets the plane at \(\left(2,2,3\right)\).

The reflection lies the same distance beyond this foot, in the opposite normal direction.

Use twice the foot minus the original point, obtaining \(\left(0,-2,-1\right)\).

blocks.html: The nearest point and the reflected point coincide only if the original point is already on the plane.

sections.title: How can a dot product give the smaller line angle?
sections.label: Use the absolute dot product
sections.intro: Line equations may choose either sign for their direction vector. Geometrically the smaller angle is independent of those choices.

blocks.html: Divide the absolute dot product by the product of the magnitudes to find its cosine.

blocks.title: Find the acute angle between two directions
blocks.prompt: Two lines have directions \(\left[\begin{matrix}1\\3\\0\end{matrix}\right]\) and \(\left[\begin{matrix}2\\-1\\1\end{matrix}\right]\). Give the exact cosine of the smaller angle between them.
blocks.hint: Use an absolute dot product to choose the smaller angle between unoriented lines.
blocks.solution:
Only the direction vectors are needed. The scale or signs of those vectors do not change the smaller angle.

Take the absolute scalar product and divide by both magnitudes.

This gives cosine \(\frac{\sqrt{15}}{30}\).

blocks.html: The positions of the lines do not affect the angle between their directions.

blocks.title: Find the acute angle between two directions

blocks.hint: Use an absolute dot product to choose the smaller angle between unoriented lines.
blocks.solution:
Only the direction vectors are needed. The scale or signs of those vectors do not change the smaller angle.

Take the absolute scalar product and divide by both magnitudes.

This gives cosine \(\frac{\sqrt{39}}{26}\).

sections.title: Why does the line–plane formula use a sine?
sections.label: Take the complement of the normal angle
sections.intro: The angle between a direction and the plane is complementary to its smaller angle with the plane normal.

blocks.html: For the smaller line–plane angle take the absolute dot product of direction and normal, divide by both magnitudes and use the result as its sine.

blocks.title: Find a line–plane angle using its complement
blocks.prompt: Find the exact sine of the smaller angle between a line in direction \(\left[\begin{matrix}1\\2\\2\end{matrix}\right]\) and \(x + 2 y + 2 z=12\).
blocks.hint: The plane’s normal is perpendicular to the plane, so use the complementary angle.
blocks.solution:
The angle to the plane is complementary to its smaller angle with the plane normal.

The cosine of that normal angle therefore equals the sine of the angle to the plane.

Divide the absolute scalar product by the product of the magnitudes, obtaining \(1\).

blocks.html: If the dot product is zero, the line is parallel to the plane, making the line–plane angle zero.

sections.title: Which vectors determine the smaller angle between planes?
sections.label: Use their normals
sections.intro: A normal fixes the orientation of a plane, so two normals identify the smaller angle between the planes.

blocks.html: Use the absolute dot product divided by both normal magnitudes as the cosine of the smaller plane angle.

blocks.title: Use the normals for the smaller angle between planes
blocks.prompt: The planes are \(x + 2 y + 2 z=12\) and \(x + y + 2 z=3\). Give the exact cosine of the smaller angle between them.

blocks.hint: Do not use the right-hand constants of the plane equations when computing an angle.
blocks.solution:
Choose one normal to each plane. Their scalar product is \(7\).

For the smaller plane angle, take the absolute value of the dot product.

Divide by the product of the two normal magnitudes to obtain \(\frac{7 \sqrt{6}}{18}\).

Only the direction vectors are needed. The scale or signs of those vectors do not change the smaller angle.

Take the absolute scalar product and divide by both magnitudes.

This gives cosine \(\frac{2 \sqrt{222}}{111}\).

extraPractice.title: Find a line–plane angle using its complement
extraPractice.prompt: Find the exact sine of the smaller angle between a line in direction \(\left[\begin{matrix}1\\3\\2\end{matrix}\right]\) and \(x + 2 y + 2 z=13\).
extraPractice.hint: The plane’s normal is perpendicular to the plane, so use the complementary angle.
extraPractice.solution:
The angle to the plane is complementary to its smaller angle with the plane normal.

The cosine of that normal angle therefore equals the sine of the angle to the plane.

Divide the absolute scalar product by the product of the magnitudes, obtaining \(\frac{11 \sqrt{14}}{42}\).

extraPractice.hint: Do not use the right-hand constants of the plane equations when computing an angle.
extraPractice.solution:
Choose one normal to each plane. Their scalar product is \(13\).

For the smaller plane angle, take the absolute value of the dot product.

Divide by the product of the two normal magnitudes to obtain \(\frac{13 \sqrt{3}}{27}\).

fp1_vectors_parameters.description: Keep exceptional parameter values when solving for a line–plane crossing, distance or coincident planes.

sections.title: What if a line–plane equation loses its parameter term?
sections.label: Test the vanishing coefficient first
sections.intro: A unique line crossing requires a non-zero coefficient of its own line parameter. A family can lose that coefficient at special values.

blocks.html: At each such value check the constant too. A zero constant contains the line, while a non-zero constant leaves a distinct parallel line.

blocks.title: Check the values that make the parameter equation vanish
blocks.prompt: Consider \(\mathbf r=\left[\begin{matrix}k\\0\\1\end{matrix}\right]+t\left[\begin{matrix}k \left(k - 3\right)\\1\\1\end{matrix}\right]\) and the plane \(x=0\). Give the value of k giving a contained line and the value giving a distinct parallel line.

fields.label: k for a distinct parallel line

blocks.hint: Check zero coefficients before dividing by a factor involving a parameter.
blocks.solution:
An intersection uses \(k+t k(k-3)=0\). The t coefficient vanishes at \(k=0\) and \(k=3\).

At zero the starting x-coordinate also vanishes, so every point of the line is in the plane.

At \(k=3\) the starting x-coordinate is non-zero, so there is no crossing.

blocks.html: Dividing by the coefficient before checking it silently loses exceptional cases.

sections.title: Why can a fixed distance give two parameter values?
sections.label: Solve both signed alternatives
sections.intro: The distance is the magnitude of a signed normal displacement. Both sides of a plane can be the same positive distance from it.

blocks.html: Use both signs when rearranging the absolute value. Test the resulting points in the complete distance relation.

blocks.title: Keep the two planes at a fixed distance
blocks.prompt: Find all real k such that \(\left(k,1,2\right)\) is at distance \(3\) from \(x + 2 y + 2 z=4\).
blocks.hint: A fixed positive distance normally gives alternatives on opposite sides of the plane.
blocks.solution:
The distance condition is \(\left|k + 2\right|=9\).

Use both signs on the right-hand side.

The two values are \(k=-11\) and \(k=7\).

blocks.html: Taking just the positive sign normally gives only one side of the plane.

sections.title: What changes when two moving directions become parallel?
sections.label: Reclassify before measuring distance
sections.intro: The vector product of two directions gives a usable normal only if the directions are non-parallel.

blocks.html: For parallel directions project a displacement perpendicular to the common direction instead. A skew limit need not equal this separate distance.

blocks.title: Recompute distance when a cross product vanishes
blocks.prompt: Find the distance between \(\mathbf r=\left[\begin{matrix}0\\0\\0\end{matrix}\right]+s\left[\begin{matrix}1\\0\\0\end{matrix}\right]\) and \(\mathbf r=\left[\begin{matrix}0\\3\\4\end{matrix}\right]+t\left[\begin{matrix}1\\k\\0\end{matrix}\right]\) for non-zero k and for k = 0.
blocks.hint: A specialised formula for skew lines cannot be applied after the directions become parallel.
blocks.solution:
For non-zero k, the directions span the xy-plane. The shortest direction is vertical and the z gap is \(4\).

At zero both directions are horizontal along x. The cross product used before is zero and cannot be normalised.

The shortest gap is now the whole yz displacement, with length \(5\).

blocks.html: Do not substitute directly into a formula that divides by a zero vector magnitude.

blocks.title: Recompute distance when a cross product vanishes
blocks.prompt: Find the distance between \(\mathbf r=\left[\begin{matrix}0\\0\\0\end{matrix}\right]+s\left[\begin{matrix}1\\0\\0\end{matrix}\right]\) and \(\mathbf r=\left[\begin{matrix}0\\5\\6\end{matrix}\right]+t\left[\begin{matrix}1\\k\\0\end{matrix}\right]\) for non-zero k and for k = 0.
blocks.hint: A specialised formula for skew lines cannot be applied after the directions become parallel.
blocks.solution:
For non-zero k, the directions span the xy-plane. The shortest direction is vertical and the z gap is \(6\).

At zero both directions are horizontal along x. The cross product used before is zero and cannot be normalised.

The shortest gap is now the whole yz displacement, with length \(\sqrt{61}\).

sections.title: When can the common part of two planes become a whole plane?
sections.label: Check whether the constraints duplicate
sections.intro: A new parameter can make a second constraint proportional to the first. Compare normals and constants together.

blocks.html: A non-parallel pair gives a line. Coincident equations describe the same plane, so testing only for a line misses that case.

blocks.title: Identify when two plane constraints become identical
blocks.prompt: For \(x + y + z=5\) and \(x \left(k - 3\right) + y + z=5\), find k for coincident planes. Otherwise give the fixed x-coordinate of their intersection.

fields.label: Fixed x-coordinate in the non-coincident case

blocks.hint: Two plane equations can collapse to one at an exceptional value.
blocks.solution:
Subtract the plane equations to obtain \((k - 4)x=0\).

If \(k=4\) this gives no new condition and the two planes coincide.

Otherwise \(x=0\) and the remaining relation gives a line in that plane.

blocks.html: When a factor relating the plane equations is zero, the corresponding coordinate need not be zero.

sections.title: How do I check which point in a family lies on the plane?
sections.label: Evaluate the original plane expression
sections.intro: A changing coordinate can make a family of points pass through a plane. Use the normal equation instead of treating the parameter as a line coefficient by default.

blocks.html: Substitute the whole point vector and solve the resulting scalar equation. Then give the requested coordinate at that parameter value.

blocks.title: Use the normal component to test a family of points
blocks.prompt: A plane has normal \(\left[\begin{matrix}2\\-1\\1\end{matrix}\right]\) and equation \(2 x - y + z=2\). For which k is \(\left(2,k,2\right)\) in the plane? Give the signed change in the left-hand side when k increases by one.
blocks.hint: Check membership by evaluating the whole plane expression.
blocks.solution:
The point lies in the plane when its scalar product with the normal is the stated constant.

This gives \(6 - k=2\) and hence \(k=4\).

Only the coefficient of the changing y-coordinate affects the signed change. It gives \(-1\).

blocks.html: Keep the fixed coordinates in the scalar product, even when only one coordinate depends on the parameter.

blocks.title: Use the normal component to test a family of points
blocks.prompt: A plane has normal \(\left[\begin{matrix}2\\-1\\1\end{matrix}\right]\) and equation \(2 x - y + z=4\). For which k is \(\left(4,k,2\right)\) in the plane? Give the signed change in the left-hand side when k increases by one.
blocks.hint: Check membership by evaluating the whole plane expression.
blocks.solution:
The point lies in the plane when its scalar product with the normal is the stated constant.

This gives \(10 - k=4\) and hence \(k=6\).

Only the coefficient of the changing y-coordinate affects the signed change. It gives \(-1\).
